title: Metaphor, Simile and Imagery
objective: After this level you can tell a metaphor from a simile and explain how an image makes a reader feel an idea.
summary: A simile compares with "like" or "as" (Burns's red, red rose); a metaphor speaks as if one thing is another ("All the world's a stage"). Both build imagery for the senses.

cards.headline: Robert Burns compared his love to a rose. One small word does the work.
cards.body: His song opens: "O my Luve's like a red, red rose, / That's newly sprung in June." Notice the "like." Take it out and you get a different kind of comparison. That tiny word is the whole difference between two of poetry's oldest tools.

items.label: Metaphor
points: No "like" or "as": one thing is the other

cards.headline: All the world's a stage
cards.body: Metaphor comes from the Greek metaphora, "a transfer": it carries one thing's qualities over to another. In As You Like It, Shakespeare's Jaques says, "All the world's a stage, / And all the men and women merely players; / They have their exits and their entrances." Not a "like" in sight. For a moment the world simply is a theater, and your life has entrances and exits.

cards.headline: Imagery: ideas you can feel
cards.body: Imagery is language that calls up the senses: sight, sound, smell, touch and taste. Similes and metaphors are two ways to build it. Burns doesn't tell you his love is lovely. He hands you a red, red rose, newly sprung in June, and lets you see it. An image gives you an experience to imagine, not just a statement to accept.

cards.headline: Comparisons: drawn
learned: Metaphor: one thing is the other

questions.prompt: "My love is like a flower" is a simile rather than a metaphor because it _____.

options.label: rhymes
options.rationale: Rhyme has nothing to do with it.

questions.explanation: A simile makes the comparison explicit with "like" or "as"; "My love is a flower" would be a metaphor.

questions.prompt: How does the metaphor "All the world's a stage" work?

options.label: It speaks of the world as a theater, with no "like" or "as"
It describes a real theater called The World
It compares the world to a stage using "like"
It repeats the same consonant sound

questions.explanation: A metaphor carries one thing's qualities over to another without "like" or "as": the world simply is a stage.

questions.prompt: In Level 7, Daphne really becomes a laurel tree. If a poet wrote "she is a laurel," what would be different?

options.label: Nothing: both are transformations
options.rationale: Only the myth has a real change.

options.label: It would be a simile, because it uses "is"
It would be a metaphor: a comparison, not a real change
It would be an image of sound
options.rationale: A laurel is something you see.

questions.explanation: In Ovid's myth the change actually happens; a metaphor only speaks as if one thing were the other.
